extracted.intended_audience: graduate students / advanced undergraduates studying algebraic geometry (Math 216)
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpts from a graduate-level algebraic geometry textbook (Ravi Vakil) giving definitions, theorems, proofs, remarks and exercises on Algebraic Hartogs’s Lemma, fiber-dimension semicontinuity, Krull theorems, and the Zariski tangent space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic Hartogs’s Lemma (11.3.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose A is a Noetherian normal integral domain. Then A = ∩_{p codimension 1} A_p (equality inside K(A)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: a rational function on a normal scheme with no poles (i.e., no poles at codimension 1 primes) is in fact regular (an element of A). Warning: few people call this Algebraic Hartogs’s Lemma; the author uses the name because it parallels the complex-analytic statement. One may generalize to Spec A a Noetherian normal scheme (A a product of Noetherian normal integral domains). See also later definitions of zeros and poles (12.5.7) and Exercise 12.5.H.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic for poles/zeros in Algebraic Hartogs
rubrics_metrics.description: If f ∈ K(A) does not lie in A_p where p has codimension 1, then f has a pole at [p]; if f lies in p A_p where p has codimension 1, then f has a zero at [p].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful interpretation: Hartogs’s Lemma says that if there are no poles of f at any codimension 1 point, then f ∈ A. This is used repeatedly when relating line bundles and divisors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral closure as intersection of valuation rings
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is a subring of a field K, then the integral closure of A in K is the intersection of all valuation rings of K containing A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference: [AtM, Cor. 5.22] for explanation and proof; this is another generalization/proper formulation related to Hartogs-type statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal of denominators (proof technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: For x ∈ K(A), define I := { r ∈ A : r x ∈ A } — the ideal of denominators of x; I measures the failure of x to be regular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use I to localize and pick a minimal prime q over I; localizing at q and analyzing containment properties of multiples of x produces contradictions when proving Algebraic Hartogs’s Lemma. The ideal-theoretic viewpoint gives a scheme-theoretic locus where x is not regular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise 11.3.L (lines on hypersurfaces — criterion for line through point)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a homogeneous degree d polynomial f(x0,...,xn) = f_d(x1,...,xn) + x0 f_{d-1}+ ... + x0^{d-1} f_1 cutting out X in P^n containing p = [1,0,...,0]: there is a line through p contained in X iff f_1 = f_2 = ... = f_{n-1} = f_d = 0 has a common zero in P^{n-1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: given a common zero [a1,...,an] the line joining p to [0,a1,...,an] lies in X. Use this and Chevalley-type genericity arguments to show generic statements about presence/absence of lines through points for hypersurfaces of various degrees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: uniruled variety (Remark 11.3.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: A projective (or proper) k-variety X is uniruled if every point p ∈ X is contained in some P^1 ⊂ X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and relations: hypersurfaces of degree at most n−1 are uniruled; degree at least n+1 (char 0) smooth hypersurfaces are not uniruled; smooth hypersurfaces of degree n are uniruled but covered by conics. Links to Fano/Calabi–Yau/general type classifications; see §21.5.5 for definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key inequality on codimensions for morphisms (Exercise 11.4.A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose π: X → Y is a morphism of locally Noetherian schemes and p ∈ X, q ∈ Y with q = π(p). Then codim_X p ≤ codim_Y q + codim_{π^{-1}(q)} p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric intuition: codimension of a point in the total space is bounded by sum of codimension in the fiber and codimension of the image in the target. Hint: choose systems of parameters for q in Y and for p in π^{-1}(q) and combine them to cut out the closed point in Spec O_{X,p}. Equality often holds for flat morphisms (see Proposition 24.5.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 11.4.1 (generic fiber pure dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: For π: X → Y a finite-type morphism of irreducible k-varieties with dim X = m and dim Y = n, there exists a nonempty open U ⊂ Y such that for all y ∈ U, the fiber π^{-1}(y) has pure dimension m − n (or is empty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: reduce to affine case, assume π dominant, work over generic point via inclusions B → A → K(A) and K(B) → K(A), use transcendence degrees and Noether normalization to produce t_i algebraically independent over K(B), clear denominators to spread out to a distinguished open D(f), and obtain a finite surjective morphism to A^{m−n}_U. Use Exercise 11.4.A and codimension = difference of dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 11.4.2 (upper semicontinuity of fiber dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) The fiber-dimension function on X (dimension of largest component of the fiber containing p) is upper semicontinuous. (b) If π is closed (e.g., proper), then the fiber-dimension function on Y is upper semicontinuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by induction on dim Y: define F_n = {points where fiber-dimension ≥ n} and show closedness. Use Proposition 11.4.1 to produce dense open where relative dimension equals r = dim X − dim Y, then reduce. Note: properness is needed for part (b) — without it counterexamples exist. Exercise 11.4.D and 11.4.E provide reductions and completion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 11.4.3 (generically finite ⇒ generally finite)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π: X → Y is a generically finite morphism of irreducible k-varieties of dimension n, then there exists a dense open V ⊂ Y above which π is finite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce to affine case. Cover X by finitely many affine opens Ui; apply finite-case exercise to find dense opens Vi where π|_{Ui} is finite; show π is closed and remove the image of the complement to get V where π is finite. Exercises 11.4.F–11.4.H guide the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of semicontinuities (11.4.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common semicontinuous phenomena: (i) fiber dimension (upper), (ii) rank of a matrix of functions (lower), (iii) rank of finite-type quasicoherent sheaf (upper), (iv) degree of a finite morphism (upper), (v) dimension of tangent space at closed points (upper), (vi) rank of cohomology groups of coherent sheaves in proper flat families (upper).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware which invariants are upper vs lower semicontinuous; (ii) is lower semicontinuous while the others listed are upper semicontinuous. This guides expectations about how invariants behave under specialization and limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension to more general bases (11.4.5–11.4.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: The previous results extend beyond varieties to locally Noetherian situations; in particular, Spec of a finitely generated Z-algebra and excellent rings inherit the properties needed so upper semicontinuity of fiber-dimension on the source holds for finite-type morphisms of locally Noetherian schemes (and locally finitely presented morphisms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key facts used: codimension = difference of dimensions (where catenary hypotheses apply), finite-type hypotheses, and the ability to 'spread out' constructions by inverting finitely many denominators. See Exercise 28.2.L for formal statements about pulling back from Spec of finitely generated Z-algebras.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Artinian module / ring and Lemma 11.5.1
rubrics_metrics.description: An A-module is Artinian if it satisfies the descending chain condition for submodules. Lemma: If A is a Noetherian ring with one prime ideal m then A is Artinian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use finite filtrations whose quotients are Artinian to deduce Artinian property. This fact is used in proofs of Krull Principal Ideal Theorem by reducing to Artinian quotients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Krull’s Principal Ideal Theorem (proof sketch 11.5.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f ∈ A and p is a minimal prime containing (f), then height(p) ≤ 1 (equivalently, minimal primes over a principal ideal have height at most 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses localization at p, construction of symbolic powers q(n) and Nakayama’s lemma to show stabilization and deduce that Aq has dimension 0. Key steps: show A/(f) is Artinian, analyze descending chain q(1)+ (f) ⊃ q(2)+ (f) ⊃ ... to get q(n) = q(n+1), localize and apply Nakayama to get q^n A_q = 0, hence dim A_q = 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Krull’s Height Theorem (proof sketch 11.5.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an ideal is generated by n elements, then any minimal prime over that ideal has height at most n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove by induction on n. Use Krull Principal Ideal Theorem for base case n=1. Reduce by localizing at p, choose q minimal under p, manipulate generators to show q is minimal over an ideal generated by n−1 elements, and apply inductive hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Zariski cotangent and tangent space (12.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a local ring (A,m), the Zariski cotangent space is m/m^2 (a vector space over A/m); the Zariski tangent space is its dual. For a scheme X and point p, T^∨_{X,p} := m/m^2 of O_{X,p} and T_{X,p} its dual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements of cotangent space are differentials; tangent vectors correspond to derivations at the point. This definition is algebraically natural and is used to measure smoothness/regularity at points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence with derivations (motivation and Exercise 12.1.A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivations at a point induce maps m/m^2 → k(p) and conversely any linear map m/m^2 → k(p) yields a derivation (satisfying Leibniz), establishing tangent space ≅ space of derivations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives the geometric intuition connecting the algebraic definition to classical notions of tangent vectors as derivations. Check Exercise 12.1.A to verify reversibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangent behavior under hypersurface quotient (Exercise 12.1.B)
rubrics_metrics.description: For A a ring and maximal ideal m, the Zariski tangent space of A/(f) at m is cut out in the Zariski tangent space of A at m by the single linear equation f (mod m^2). Consequently, the tangent-space dimension of Spec A/(f) at [m] is either that of Spec A at [m] or one less (interpreting infinite dimensions appropriately).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the 'Krull Principal Ideal Theorem for tangent spaces' — picking off linear terms corresponds to cutting by one linear equation; use it to diagnose singularities and to compute tangent spaces in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Zariski tangent space to detect non-principal codimension-1 ideals (examples 12.1.3–12.1.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: In A = k[x,y,z]/(xy − z^2), the ideal (x,z) is not principal. At the cone point m=(x,y,z), dim T_{Spec A,m} = 3, but dim T_{Spec A/(x,z),m} = 1, while Exercise 12.1.B implies Spec A/(f) must have tangent dimension ≥ 2, contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tangent-space dimension jumping up (larger than expected) is a signature of singularity; use tangent-space comparisons to deduce impossibility of principality or smoothness. Alternative proofs may use gradings/associated graded rings where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic formal properties of tangent spaces for unions/intersections (Exercise 12.1.C)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Y and Z are closed subschemes of X containing p, then: (a) T_{Z,p} ⊂ T_{X,p} as a κ(p)-vector subspace. (b) T_{Y∩Z,p} = T_{Y,p} ∩ T_{Z,p} (scheme-theoretic intersection). (c) T_{Y∪Z,p} contains the span of T_{Y,p} and T_{Z,p} (scheme-theoretic union). (d) T_{Y∪Z,p} can be strictly larger than that span.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These statements describe how tangent spaces behave under basic set-theoretic and scheme-theoretic operations; part (d) warns that unions can enlarge tangent spaces beyond the naive linear span, an important anti-pattern when reasoning geometrically.
